bib.title: Knowledge or Reasoning? A Close Look at How LLMs Think Across Domains

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: All 17 pages, 55,252 chars, read in full (body, limitations, both appendices, prompts, Table 4). Only the reference list was skimmed. Figures 6 and 8 are text-extracted bar values and were not viewed as images.

SOURCE: "Knowledge or Reasoning? A Close Look at How LLMs Think Across Domains". First author Juncheng Wu (UC Santa Cruz). Co-authors: Sheng Liu and James Zou (Stanford), Hang Yu (Tongji), Haoqin Tu, Xiaoke Huang, Cihang Xie, Yuyin Zhou (UCSC). arXiv:2506.02126v1 [cs.CL], 2 Jun 2025. The PDF says "Preprint. Under review." so it is a preprint. Code: github.com/UCSC-VLAA/ReasoningEval.

CORE CLAIM: Final-answer accuracy hides two separable things. One is whether each reasoning step uses correct facts (Knowledge Index, KI). The other is whether each step moves the model toward the answer (Information Gain, InfoGain). Training methods and domains affect the two differently. Method: GPT-4o splits each chain of thought into steps. InfoGain is the mean per-step drop in the perplexity of the gold answer, scored by an untrained Qwen2.5-7B. KI is the fraction of steps that GPT-4o judges consistent with retrieved reference facts (p.4-5).

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all Qwen2.5-7B family; the paper reports no n, no seeds and no confidence intervals):
1. Table 1, medical, 5 benchmarks averaged, SFT only: Qwen-Base 52.79% accuracy vs Qwen-R1 (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) 38.07%. With SFT+RL: Qwen-Base 60.02% vs Qwen-R1 31.48%. Average KI is 63.40 vs 56.49 for SFT only and 64.23 vs 54.29 for SFT+RL. Average InfoGain is near-equal (2.347 vs 2.249 for SFT only, 2.348 vs 2.309 for SFT+RL).
2. Fig 6b, SFT vs untrained base: medical InfoGain 0.39 to 0.22 and math 0.13 to 0.09. The text calls this "an average reduction of 37.1%". The abstract says 38.9% and the intro says 38.9%. The paper is inconsistent on this figure.
3. KI on medical benchmarks, Qwen-Base (Sec 4.2): base 49.71, RL-ed 60.24, SFT-ed 63.40. RL on top of the base model raises KI by 12.4 points on average, and by 2.2 points when added after SFT (Fig 8).
4. Correlation with accuracy across 5 medical benchmarks (Fig 5, Sec 4.1): the average-across-tasks correlation of KI with accuracy is 0.998, "0.3 higher than that of reasoning". On PubMedQA, KI correlates 0.897 vs InfoGain 0.465. MedQA and MedXpert are above 0.9 for both.
5. Accuracy by domain (Sec 4.2, Fig 6a): medical, SFT-ed 49.8% > RL-ed 49.8% > base 48.2% (the text states "4.6% and 6.2%" gains, which these numbers do not match). Math, RL-ed 61.7% > SFT-ed 51.9% > base 40.5%.

INCONSISTENCIES IN THE TEXT (do not copy uncritically):
- Sec 4.1 says "54.06% vs. 31.48%" for the SFT+RL gap, but Table 1 gives 60.02%.
- The "22.6% increase" is not reconcilable with Table 1 either.
- The 37.1% vs 38.9% InfoGain drop noted above.
- The intro says "6.2% average KI increase" for SFT, but Sec 4.2 uses 6.2% for an accuracy gain.
- Table 1 InfoGain looks like scaled raw units (MedMCQA about 9), while Fig 6 uses 0 to 1 values. The scaling is unexplained.

QUOTES:
- "Knowledge and Reasoning Should be Two Distinct Evaluation Aspects for LLMs." (p.6)
- "Accuracy alone fails to capture these nuances." (Fig 1 caption, p.2)
- Table 2 (appendix, p.13) shows the existing ROSCOE semantic-alignment metrics are flat across base, SFT and RL models (Faithfulness-Step avg 0.781, 0.781, 0.781), while KI and InfoGain move. This is the paper's argument that older step metrics cannot discriminate.

LIMITS (conceded and not shown):
- Authors concede only Qwen 7B models were tested and broader models are needed. Only math and medicine were tested.
- GPT-4o does the step splitting, the knowledge extraction and the consistency judging. The paper reports no human validation of those judgments and no judge-agreement figure.
- KI is computed for medical benchmarks only, because there is no knowledge base for math. The math side therefore has InfoGain only.
- No seeds, variance or significance tests. Gaps such as KI 64.2 vs 63.4 are small and untested.
- The causal story is conjecture. For example, the claim that RL "prunes" wrong knowledge rests on one case study (Fig 9), and the R1-conflict explanation is stated as "may stem from".
- Correlations are over only 5 benchmark points, so the "knowledge-dominated" reading is thin.
- The KI reference source is described as "a widely-employed... medical database" (and textbooks, citing MedQA [19]), which is vague.
- The RL setup is PPO with a sparse +1/0 verifier reward, so the findings may not hold for other RL recipes.
- The InfoGain judge is the untrained Qwen2.5-7B, so the metric depends on that model.

BUILDS ON: ROSCOE (Golovneva 2022), ReCEval (Prasad 2023), RCoT (Xue 2023), Verify-and-Edit (Zhao 2023), HuatuoGPT-o1 (Chen 2024, medical-o1 data), RLHFlow (Dong 2024), DeepSeek-R1-Distill (DeepSeek-AI 2025), "SFT memorizes, RL generalizes" (Chu 2025), Panickssery 2024 (self-preference bias, the reason for a separate PPL model), Brown 2020 (perplexity).

BEST-FIT SECTION in 09-reading-results.md: "Read the transcripts" (line 230), as a pointer to step-level scoring of reasoning traces: right final answer, wrong facts, or redundant steps. The accuracy-vs-process point also fits as a short sub-point in "Slice before you conclude" (line 189). Note headings checked: the note is about pass-rate statistics, so the paper fits only as a sidebar, not as statistical evidence. If a separate home is wanted, 05-llm-as-judge.md or 04-graders.md fits better, because the method is an LLM-judged step grader. Not checked: the contents of those two notes.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1, p.2, "Reasoning and Knowledge are Different Evaluation Aspects for LLMs". One diabetes trace shows a step with wrong knowledge that still advances the answer, and a correct but redundant step. Fig 2 (p.3, pipeline) is the alternative.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Text extraction is clean, except that table and bar-chart values are flattened.
